Recreation Region: Bankhead National Forest
Clear Creek Recreation Area
Current Conditions
The Boat Ramp is open all year with a Day Pass to the Boat Ramp.
The Clear Creek Recreation Area has become one of Alabama's most popular recreation areas and has many repeat visitors. The Bankhead National Forest’s largest recreation area, Clear Creek is in Winston County about 13 miles north of Jasper, ALlabama and was constructed on the shore of Lewis Smith Lake giving direct recreational access to the lake via the day use boat launch, to boating, water skiing, personal watercraft use, as well as fishing for largemouth bass, striped bass, and crappie. With many modern conveniences, it offers facilities for individual and group camping, picnicking, swimming, boat launching, hiking, and biking.
Visit Recreation.gov to make a reservation. Camping at this location is by reservation only. For additional information please call 205-300-1463.
Check-out time for Clear Creek is no later than 12:00pm the day of departure. Check-in time is no earlier than 2:00pm. This 2 hour window allows our staff adequate time to clean and maintain each site.
The campground itself has four paved loops with paved parking spurs, and offers 102 RV campsites, including 32 double sites; 11 of these are pull-through sites. Each campsite has water and electrical hookups, a fire ring, picnic table, and lantern posts. All campsites have 50-amp and 30-amp electrical service. There is a trailer dump station located within the recreation area. Each of the four loops has a bathhouse with flush toilets and showers. All sites are level and spacious; Single campsites accommodate up to six people and two vehicles; double sites up to twelve people and four vehicles. No garbage dumpsters are in the campground; users are required to pack out trash and deposit it in the dumpsters by the dump station. An entrance station with an electronic gate is available to control access to the campground. Two group camping areas, available by reservation only, accommodate up to 25 tent campers each and share a bathhouse with flushing toilets and showers.
The day use portion of the recreation area focuses on the swimming beach, served by a bathhouse with flushing toilets and showers. Next to the beach is a 50-person group picnic pavilion, with a flush toilet. On the other side of the beach lies a picnic area with 53 family units, all connected by newly paved paths. On the point, adjacent to the lake, are two more 50-person picnic pavilions, served by a nearby flush toilet. A 1.5-mile paved bicycle trail connects the campground to the day use area. Also, there is the 2.5-mile recently paved Raven Cliffs hiking trail in the day use area. Use of the picnic pavilions is by reservation only; users also pay the day use fee as they park in the facility. A year-round boat launch is available with an SST vault toilet and boat/trailer parking.
Facilities: All facilities are wheelchair-accessible. Flush toilets, drinking water and showers are offered for both campers and day use visitors. The campground offers standard sites with electric and water hook-ups, as well as tent-only non-electric sites for groups. Sites contain paved parking spurs, picnic tables, grills and tent pads.

Coleman Lake Recreation Area
The newly renovated Coleman Lake Recreation Area is peacefully nestled into the Talladega mountains. For recreationists who want to get away from the crowds, but want a few modern conveniences, Coleman Lake Recreation Area is your place to be. There are 39 campsites with water and electrical hookups, bathhouses, 29 picnicking units,  a 21-acre lake and access to the Pinhoti Trail. Two new comfort stations and seven camping sites are fully accessible for the physically challenged. Most sites will accommodate recreational vehicles up to 35 feet in length. A picnic shelter that seats 40 is available on a first come, first serve basis, or it can be reserved for $15.

Current Conditions
Open
Payne Lake Recreation Area offers the outdoor enthusiasts solitude, a scenic lake, and picturesque campsites. Payne Lake Recreation Area has one swimming beach and two bathhouses for users of the recreation area. Each bathhouse has restrooms and showers. Camping is permitted at 26 developed sites along the shoreline of the 110-acre Payne Lake. Each site has a picnic table, cooking or fire circle, and tent or trailer pad.
Payne Lake Recreation Area is open year-round and offers boating, fishing, picnicking and swimming opportunities for Forest users. A trailer dump station is located in the campground.

Drinking water is no longer available at Andrews Cove Campground. The campground well system is being decommissioned due to the high cost of maintaining and operating the aging infrastructure.

Andrews Cove Recreation Area in White County offers a cool mountain stream and a peaceful atmosphere, and is only 15 minutes from the popular alpine village of Helen, Georgia.

14 Day Camping Limit
Camping or maintaining a campsite on National Forest System lands within any area of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest exceeding an aggregate of 14 days in any 30-day period is prohibited. Once a combination of any 14 days has been reached, individuals must remove their property and leave the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest until the end of the 30-day period.

semantic.bounded_official_text:
ATV and OHV - Call Before You Haul
Motorized trails close when conditions are wet to prevent trail damage and erosion into streams. Check the status of your favorite trail or Call Before You Haul.
1. Keep It Safe
- Wear proper safety gear.
- Maintain a safe speed.
- Stay alert.
2. Keep It Legal
- Know where you can ride. Keep a current map.
- Verify what trails are open and when.
- Learn and follow the rules. Get an OHV pass.
3. Keep on the Trails
- Travel only on routes designated for your use.
- Get maps of designated routes from the Forest Service.
- Obey signs and temporary postings.
4. Keep The Privilege
- Respect the environment. Tread Lightly!®
- Be courteous to other trail users.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest begins prescribed fires
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest begins prescribed fires
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has begun prescribed fire operations, pending all required approvals. We estimate this work to continue through May as weather conditions allow. We use prescribed fires to help reduce overgrown vegetation to help protect local communities, infrastructure and natural resources from wildfires.
Those areas may close to the public for several days for public safety. Watch for warning signs along roads near all prescribed fire areas before and during burns.
Residents may experience smoke during the prescribed burns. When driving, slow down and turn on your headlights when you encounter smoke on the road.
We will evaluate weather conditions in the hours before a burn begins. If conditions warrant, scheduled prescribed fire activities may be canceled.
Stay informed about the scheduled prescribed fires through this website and Facebook.
View planned and active prescribed fire on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest by visiting the Southern Region Prescribed Burn Accomplishment Tracker at: https://arcg.is/nmXrr2.
Learn more about prescribed fire management: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r08/chattahoochee-oconee/fire/management

semantic.title: Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has reopened Duncan Ridge Road (FSR 39) following completion of culvert replacement work at Mulky Creek on the Blue Ridge Ranger District.
The project replaced an aging culvert at the creek crossing to improve long-term road reliability, protect water quality and support healthier watershed conditions in the area. The upgraded crossing is designed to better withstand heavy rain events while also improving aquatic organism passage through Mulky Creek.
While the road is now fully reopened to vehicle traffic, visitors are asked to avoid using the nearby dispersed campsite adjacent to the project area until soil stabilization and vegetation growth are fully established. The temporary closure of the campsite will help protect restoration efforts and reduce the risk of erosion or resource damage while the disturbed area recovers.
Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.
For additional information or questions about access in the area, please contact the Blue Ridge Ranger District. The Forest Service appreciates the public’s patience and cooperation throughout the project and restoration process.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Old CCC Camp Road / Forest Service Road 18 – Temporary Closure Beginning September 8
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Old CCC Camp Road / Forest Service Road 18 – Temporary Closure Beginning September 8
Road paving crews will be working through November to pave the section of roadway that runs directly alongside Holly Creek. This project will help reduce ongoing erosion and protect water quality in one of the state’s most important aquatic habitats.
The first unpaved half‑mile of Old CCC Camp Road/Forest Service Road 18—from the Dill Creek Bridge to the Holly Creek Bridge—will be closed to through traffic beginning September 8. Local residential access will be maintained throughout the project except for a two-day period when paving will occur.
We appreciate your patience while this work is underway and encourage visitors to plan ahead for closures, temporary delays or detours in the area.
This closure will affect access to the Emery Creek Trailhead.

semantic.title: Peavine Sheeds Road Closure for repairs
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Peavine Sheeds Road Closure for repairs
Phase one road construction on Peavine Sheeds Creek Road/FS 221, on the Cherokee National Forest north of the Jacks River bridge into Tennessee will be closed heading west from July  20 – Sept 14.
Phase two construction beginning September 15-January 4 will close Peavine Sheeds Creek Road/FS 221 east,  from the Jacks River Bridge to the northern end of Big Frog Road/FS 62. This will restrict access to the Beech Bottom Trailhead from the south end of Big Frog Road/FS 62 during the closure. semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.

Before riding your UTV, Educate Yourself! Obtain a map (motor vehicle use map) of your destination and determine which areas are open to UTVs. Respected Access is Open Access! By practicing responsible outdoor recreation, we can keep our favorite areas open to the public. By treating land access with respect, we can help keep our favorite trails, parks and forests open, healthy and beautiful. So get out and enjoy yourself with us responsibly!

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has begun prescribed fire operations, pending all required approvals. We estimate this work to continue through May as weather conditions allow. We use prescribed fires to help reduce overgrown vegetation to help protect local communities, infrastructure and natural resources from wildfires.
Those areas may close to the public for several days for public safety. Watch for warning signs along roads near all prescribed fire areas before and during burns.
Residents may experience smoke during the prescribed burns. When driving, slow down and turn on your headlights when you encounter smoke on the road.
We will evaluate weather conditions in the hours before a burn begins. If conditions warrant, scheduled prescribed fire activities may be canceled.
Stay informed about the scheduled prescribed fires through this website and Facebook.
View planned and active prescribed fire on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest by visiting the Southern Region Prescribed Burn Accomplishment Tracker at: https://arcg.is/nmXrr2.
Learn more about prescribed fire management: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r08/chattahoochee-oconee/fire/management

semantic.title: Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has reopened Duncan Ridge Road (FSR 39) following completion of culvert replacement work at Mulky Creek on the Blue Ridge Ranger District.
The project replaced an aging culvert at the creek crossing to improve long-term road reliability, protect water quality and support healthier watershed conditions in the area. The upgraded crossing is designed to better withstand heavy rain events while also improving aquatic organism passage through Mulky Creek.
While the road is now fully reopened to vehicle traffic, visitors are asked to avoid using the nearby dispersed campsite adjacent to the project area until soil stabilization and vegetation growth are fully established. The temporary closure of the campsite will help protect restoration efforts and reduce the risk of erosion or resource damage while the disturbed area recovers.
Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.
For additional information or questions about access in the area, please contact the Blue Ridge Ranger District. The Forest Service appreciates the public’s patience and cooperation throughout the project and restoration process.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.
Alert Start Date: April 23, 2026
Alert End Date:
May 4, 2026
Order Number: 08-03-00-26-04
Contact Information
Contact Name:

770-297-3000
Contact Email:sm.fs.chattoconeenf@usda.gov
Associated Documents
ORDER NUMBER 08-03-00-26-04
Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).
Possessing, discharging, or using any kind of firework or other pyrotechnic device. 36 CFR
261.52(b).
Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.
EXEMPTIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.
Executed in Gainesville, Georgia, this 23rd day of April 2026.
JUDY TOPPINS
Forest Supervisor
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest
ENFORCEMENT
Violation of these prohibitions is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000 for an individual or $10,000 for an organization, imprisonment for not more than 6 months, or both. (16 U.S.C. 551 and 18 U.S.C. 3559 and 3571).

semantic.title: UTV Education for Forest Visitors
semantic.bounded_official_text:
UTV Education for Forest Visitors
Contact(s): Chatsworth 706-695-6736 Blairsville 706-745-6928 Lakemont 706-754-6221 Eatonton 706-485-7110
Before riding your UTV, Educate Yourself! Obtain a map (motor vehicle use map) of your destination and determine which areas are open to UTVs. Respected Access is Open Access! By practicing responsible outdoor recreation, we can keep our favorite areas open to the public. By treating land access with respect, we can help keep our favorite trails, parks and forests open, healthy and beautiful. So get out and enjoy yourself with us responsibly!
Please note that Georgia House Bill 121 does not allow MPOHVs, low speed vehicles, and motorized carts to be driven on Forest Service Roads on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. 40-6-362) restricts operation of multipurpose off-highway vehicles to highways that are part of a county road system. To be legal for use on Forest Service Roads, vehicles must be licensed under State law for general operation on ALL public roads within the State. Forest Service roads are not considered county roads.
Motorized trails close when conditions are wet to prevent trail damage and erosion into streams. Check the status of your favorite trail or Call Before You Haul.
1. Keep It Safe
- Wear proper safety gear.
- Maintain a safe speed.
- Stay alert.
2. Keep It Legal
- Know where you can ride. Keep a current map.
- Verify what trails are open and when.
- Learn and follow the rules. Get an OHV pass.
3. Keep on the Trails
- Travel only on routes designated for your use.
- Get maps of designated routes from the Forest Service.
- Obey signs and temporary postings.
4. Keep The Privilege
- Respect the environment. Tread Lightly!®
- Be courteous to other trail users.

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

Site Open

Low Gap Campground
Current Conditions
Low Gap Campground has reopened, following replacement of the restroom facilities.
Camping is by Reservation Only. There is no First Come/First Service. Reservations are done by contacting: www.recreation.gov or by calling (877) 444-6777.
Located within the Chattahoochee Wildlife Management Area and veiled by the Mark Trail Wilderness. This 13-site developed campground is as close as it gets to a dispersed camping experience with amenities. This clandestine campground is best known for its plethora of opportunities in camping, fishing, hiking, hunting, and simply basking in the light of the natural world. Low Gap is another one of our campgrounds located only a few miles from Georgia's much loved vacation destination, the alpine village of Helen, Georgia.
The area is host to some of the most scenic views. If hiking is in your plans the National Scenic Appalachian Trail has two main entry points near the area. Other favorite nearby hiking areas are Ravens Cliff Falls, Dukes Creek Falls, and Anna Ruby Falls. All are only a short drive from this campground. If you like wetting fishing lines there is fishing is available in the campground, and along the nearby Chattahoochee River.
Visitors should be aware that drinking water is no longer available at Low Gap Campground. Visitors planning to camp at Low Gap should plan to bring their own drinking water.
The Forest Service remains committed to maintaining recreation opportunities across the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest and appreciates the public’s understanding as we manage facilities responsibly.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.

ORDER NUMBER 08-03-00-26-04
Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).
Possessing, discharging, or using any kind of firework or other pyrotechnic device. 36 CFR
261.52(b).
Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.
EXEMPTIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.
Executed in Gainesville, Georgia, this 23rd day of April 2026.
JUDY TOPPINS
Forest Supervisor
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest
ENFORCEMENT
Violation of these prohibitions is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000 for an individual or $10,000 for an organization, imprisonment for not more than 6 months, or both. (16 U.S.C. 551 and 18 U.S.C. 3559 and 3571).

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

Alert End Date:
May 4, 2026
Order Number: 08-03-00-26-04
Contact Information
Contact Name:
Public Affairs
Contact Number:
770-297-3000
Contact Email:sm.fs.chattoconeenf@usda.gov
Associated Documents
ORDER NUMBER 08-03-00-26-04
Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).
Possessing, discharging, or using any kind of firework or other pyrotechnic device. 36 CFR
261.52(b).
Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.
EXEMPTIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.
Executed in Gainesville, Georgia, this 23rd day of April 2026.
JUDY TOPPINS
Forest Supervisor
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest
ENFORCEMENT
Violation of these prohibitions is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000 for an individual or $10,000 for an organization, imprisonment for not more than 6 months, or both. (16 U.S.C. 551 and 18 U.S.C. 3559 and 3571).

ATV and OHV - Call Before You Haul
Motorized trails close when conditions are wet to prevent trail damage and erosion into streams. Check the status of your favorite trail or Call Before You Haul.
1. Keep It Safe
- Wear proper safety gear.
- Maintain a safe speed.
- Stay alert.
2. Keep It Legal
- Know where you can ride. Keep a current map.
- Verify what trails are open and when.
- Learn and follow the rules. Get an OHV pass.
3. Keep on the Trails
- Travel only on routes designated for your use.
- Get maps of designated routes from the Forest Service.
- Obey signs and temporary postings.
4. Keep The Privilege
- Respect the environment. Tread Lightly!®
- Be courteous to other trail users.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest begins prescribed fires
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest begins prescribed fires
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has begun prescribed fire operations, pending all required approvals. We estimate this work to continue through May as weather conditions allow. We use prescribed fires to help reduce overgrown vegetation to help protect local communities, infrastructure and natural resources from wildfires.
Those areas may close to the public for several days for public safety. Watch for warning signs along roads near all prescribed fire areas before and during burns.
Residents may experience smoke during the prescribed burns. When driving, slow down and turn on your headlights when you encounter smoke on the road.
We will evaluate weather conditions in the hours before a burn begins. If conditions warrant, scheduled prescribed fire activities may be canceled.
Stay informed about the scheduled prescribed fires through this website and Facebook.
View planned and active prescribed fire on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest by visiting the Southern Region Prescribed Burn Accomplishment Tracker at: https://arcg.is/nmXrr2.
Learn more about prescribed fire management: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r08/chattahoochee-oconee/fire/management

semantic.title: Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has reopened Duncan Ridge Road (FSR 39) following completion of culvert replacement work at Mulky Creek on the Blue Ridge Ranger District.
The project replaced an aging culvert at the creek crossing to improve long-term road reliability, protect water quality and support healthier watershed conditions in the area. The upgraded crossing is designed to better withstand heavy rain events while also improving aquatic organism passage through Mulky Creek.
While the road is now fully reopened to vehicle traffic, visitors are asked to avoid using the nearby dispersed campsite adjacent to the project area until soil stabilization and vegetation growth are fully established. The temporary closure of the campsite will help protect restoration efforts and reduce the risk of erosion or resource damage while the disturbed area recovers.
Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.
For additional information or questions about access in the area, please contact the Blue Ridge Ranger District. The Forest Service appreciates the public’s patience and cooperation throughout the project and restoration process.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Residual Impacts from Recent Winter Storms
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Residual Impacts from Recent Winter Storms
Recent winter weather events affected portions of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. While crews have made significant progress clearing hazards and restoring access, visitors may still encounter downed trees, debris, or minor damage on some forest roads, trails, and recreation sites.
Conditions can vary widely by location. Some areas may appear fully open while others continue to experience localized impacts. Visitors are encouraged to plan ahead and use caution when traveling on the forest. If you have questions about a specific trail, road, or recreation site, please contact the nearest ranger district office for the most current conditions.
We appreciate the public’s patience as employees continue restoration work to ensure safe access across the forest.

semantic.title: Rough Ridge Trail 12 closed (Cohutta Wilderness)
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Rough Ridge Trail 12 closed (Cohutta Wilderness)
The Rough Ridge Trail (#12) in the Cohutta Wilderness (Conasauga Ranger District) is temporarily closed for public safety.
Hurricane Helene’s high winds and heavy rainfall have compounded ongoing changes to the Wilderness resulting from the 2016 drought and wildfires. These combined impacts have created dense understory growth and extensive blowdowns, resulting in hazardous trail conditions for hikers.
The trail will remain closed until they can be cleared by trail crews and volunteers.
Hickory Ridge Trail has reopened after crews and volunteers restored access by clearing downed trees.

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.
Alert Start Date: April 23, 2026
Alert End Date:
May 4, 2026
Order Number: 08-03-00-26-04
Contact Information
Contact Name:
Public Affairs
Contact Number:
770-297-3000
Contact Email:sm.fs.chattoconeenf@usda.gov
Associated Documents
ORDER NUMBER 08-03-00-26-04
Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).
Possessing, discharging, or using any kind of firework or other pyrotechnic device. 36 CFR
261.52(b).
Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.
EXEMPTIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.
Executed in Gainesville, Georgia, this 23rd day of April 2026.
JUDY TOPPINS
Forest Supervisor
Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest
ENFORCEMENT
Violation of these prohibitions is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000 for an individual or $10,000 for an organization, imprisonment for not more than 6 months, or both. (16 U.S.C. 551 and 18 U.S.C. 3559 and 3571).

semantic.title: UTV Education for Forest Visitors
semantic.bounded_official_text:
UTV Education for Forest Visitors
Contact(s): Chatsworth 706-695-6736 Blairsville 706-745-6928 Lakemont 706-754-6221 Eatonton 706-485-7110
Before riding your UTV, Educate Yourself! Obtain a map (motor vehicle use map) of your destination and determine which areas are open to UTVs. Respected Access is Open Access! By practicing responsible outdoor recreation, we can keep our favorite areas open to the public. By treating land access with respect, we can help keep our favorite trails, parks and forests open, healthy and beautiful. So get out and enjoy yourself with us responsibly!
Please note that Georgia House Bill 121 does not allow MPOHVs, low speed vehicles, and motorized carts to be driven on Forest Service Roads on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. 40-6-362) restricts operation of multipurpose off-highway vehicles to highways that are part of a county road system. To be legal for use on Forest Service Roads, vehicles must be licensed under State law for general operation on ALL public roads within the State. Forest Service roads are not considered county roads.
Motorized trails close when conditions are wet to prevent trail damage and erosion into streams. Check the status of your favorite trail or Call Before You Haul.
1. Keep It Safe
- Wear proper safety gear.
- Maintain a safe speed.
- Stay alert.
2. Keep It Legal
- Know where you can ride. Keep a current map.
- Verify what trails are open and when.
- Learn and follow the rules. Get an OHV pass.
3. Keep on the Trails
- Travel only on routes designated for your use.
- Get maps of designated routes from the Forest Service.
- Obey signs and temporary postings.
4. Keep The Privilege
- Respect the environment. Tread Lightly!®
- Be courteous to other trail users.

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.

Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).

261.52(b).

EXEMPTIONS

Before riding your UTV, Educate Yourself! Obtain a map (motor vehicle use map) of your destination and determine which areas are open to UTVs. Respected Access is Open Access! By practicing responsible outdoor recreation, we can keep our favorite areas open to the public. By treating land access with respect, we can help keep our favorite trails, parks and forests open, healthy and beautiful. So get out and enjoy yourself with us responsibly!
Please note that Georgia House Bill 121 does not allow MPOHVs, low speed vehicles, and motorized carts to be driven on Forest Service Roads on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. Georgia law (O.C.G.A. 40-6-362) restricts operation of multipurpose off-highway vehicles to highways that are part of a county road system. To be legal for use on Forest Service Roads, vehicles must be licensed under State law for general operation on ALL public roads within the State. Forest Service roads are not considered county roads.
Motorized trails close when conditions are wet to prevent trail damage and erosion into streams. Check the status of your favorite trail or Call Before You Haul.

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

Rock Creek Recreation Area
Current Conditions
Come enjoy your National Forests!
Rock Creek Recreation Area is named for the creek that runs alongside this developed recreation site.
The picnic facilities, stream-fed swimming pool and bathhouse were originally built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the early 1930s. Camping facilities were constructed by the US Forest Service in the early 1960s.
Rock Creek is a welcome respite from the summer heat in the valley, cooled by cold air flowing down from Unaka Mountain and protected from the hot sun by large trees. Situated among tall oaks, maples, hemlocks and rhododendron, these sites give the feel of deep woods privacy while offering electric hookups, RV sites, double sites, walk-in tent sites, and multiple bathhouses.
A creek-fed swimming hole, seasonal campfire programs, a rugged hiking trail into Unaka Mountain Wilderness,  an easy bicycle trail and short nature trails are among the activities you can choose during your visit.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project

Duncan Ridge Road reopens following culvert replacement project
The Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest has reopened Duncan Ridge Road (FSR 39) following completion of culvert replacement work at Mulky Creek on the Blue Ridge Ranger District.
The project replaced an aging culvert at the creek crossing to improve long-term road reliability, protect water quality and support healthier watershed conditions in the area. The upgraded crossing is designed to better withstand heavy rain events while also improving aquatic organism passage through Mulky Creek.
While the road is now fully reopened to vehicle traffic, visitors are asked to avoid using the nearby dispersed campsite adjacent to the project area until soil stabilization and vegetation growth are fully established. The temporary closure of the campsite will help protect restoration efforts and reduce the risk of erosion or resource damage while the disturbed area recovers.
Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.
For additional information or questions about access in the area, please contact the Blue Ridge Ranger District. The Forest Service appreciates the public’s patience and cooperation throughout the project and restoration process.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.
Alert Start Date: April 23, 2026
Alert End Date:
May 4, 2026

ORDER NUMBER 08-03-00-26-04
Forest Order
PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.
Building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire, including charcoal-based fire whether contained in a grill or not. 36 CFR 261.52(a).
Possessing, discharging, or using any kind of firework or other pyrotechnic device. 36 CFR
261.52(b).
Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.
EXEMPTIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.
Executed in Gainesville, Georgia, this 23rd day of April 2026.
JUDY TOPPINS
Forest Supervisor

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

semantic.title: Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Spring 2026 Forest-wide Fire Restrictions
The purpose and need of this Fire Restriction Closure Order is to prohibit activities relating to building, maintaining, or attending a fire (including charcoal fires) within unauthorized areas on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District. This also includes any use of explosives, fireworks, or other pyrotechnics devices.
Due to exceptional drought conditions and persistently low relative humidity, there is a need to ensure that no unauthorized fire-related activities occur across National Forest System Lands to prevent the endangerment of persons and property. There is also a need to help ensure the health and safety of the public as well as employees engaged in limiting the use of fire-related activities and/or fire suppression.

PROHIBITIONS
Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50 (a) and (b), for the protection of the public and natural resources, the
following acts or omissions are prohibited on all NFS lands of the Chattahoochee-Oconee National
Forests comprising the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattooga River Ranger District, Conasauga Ranger District, and Oconee Ranger District (see map; Exhibit A). The provisions shall remain in effect from April 23, 2026, through June 01, 2026, or until terminated by an authorized Forest Service official, whichever occurs first.

Note: Commercially available gas stoves (camp stoves) are permitted and such devices are excluded from this restriction.

Pursuant to 36 CFR 261.50(e), the following persons are exempt from this Order:
1. Persons with a permit specifically authorizing the otherwise prohibited act or omission.
2. Any Federal, State or Local Law Enforcement Officer or member of an organized rescue or fire fighting force in the performance of an official duty.
These prohibitions are in addition to the general prohibitions in 36 CFR Part 261, Subpart A.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.

By practicing responsible outdoor recreation, we can keep our favorite areas open to the public. semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr

semantic.title: Wildfire Prevention
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Wildfire Prevention
Wildfire activity has picked up across north and central Georgia over the past couple of weeks, and conditions remain dry. As you enjoy your time on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest, a few small choices can make a big difference in preventing human-caused fires.
• Keep campfires small, attended, and fully out before you leave. If it’s too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave.
• Avoid parking or idling vehicles on tall, dry grass—hot exhaust systems can ignite vegetation.
• Secure trailer chains to prevent dragging and sparks along roadways.
• Never burn debris on or near national forest land.
• Dispose of cigarettes and matches responsibly—never toss them on the ground or out a vehicle window.
For more tips and regional fire-prevention guidance, visit:
• U.S. Forest Service – Fire Prevention: https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/fire/safety
• Georgia Forestry Commission – Fire Safety:https://gatrees.org/wildfire/fire-safety/
• Ready.gov – Wildfire Preparedness: https://www.ready.gov/wildfires
Your care keeps our communities, firefighters, and forests safer. Thanks for helping reduce new fire starts while conditions remain elevated.

Wildcat 2 campground is closed due to road damage.

Wildcat Road has sustained 4 slides in recent years (with the first slide happening in 2019). Due to the risk of additional slides, the road has been closed in the interest of public safety. Although the winding road leading to the campground is not trailer or RV-friendly, the payoff of landing a night in this environment is pure delight. These developed tent camping-only campgrounds are buried deep in the North Georgia Mountains west of Lake Burton and along the headwaters of Wildcat Creek. The creek, seasonally stocked with rainbow trout, runs directly adjacent to the campsites and provides an astounding setting, so be prepared to capture nature at its best, and bring your camera. On clear nights the stars appear to be just an arm’s reach away!

semantic.title: Be Bear-Aware!
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Be Bear-Aware!
Camping season is bear-aware season. It's crucial to store food and scented items properly and know what to do if you encounter a bear.
Bears are curious, hungry, and have a keen sense of smell, so they are attracted to food, toothpaste, soap, and shampoo. To reduce the odds of having a bear encounter, at developed campgrounds, keep food and scented items stored in coolers in vehicles and never leave food out for long periods of time. Hikers are strongly encouraged, and in some parts of the forest are required, to use bear resistant containers.
Bears quickly lose their fear of humans when they are fed, either deliberately by campers or when campers leave food unsecured. Habituated bears have to be euthanized as relocation is ineffective.
More information is available - https://gadnr.org/if-you-know-you-know-being-bearwise-knowing-what-do-if-you-see-black-bear.

Visitors traveling in the Duncan Ridge area should continue using caution around the project site and follow any posted signs or barriers associated with the restoration area.

semantic.title: Flash Flood Awareness
semantic.bounded_official_text:
Flash Flood Awareness
Recent heavy rains have saturated the ground and raised water levels in rivers and streams. Flash flooding can occur with little or no warning, especially in low-lying areas, stream channels, and valleys. Conditions may remain hazardous even after rainfall ends.
Avoid riverbanks and streambeds. Stay at least 50 feet from the water’s edge. Stay out of valleys and low-lying terrain. Flash floods can happen even if rain occurs upstream. Do not camp in dry streambeds or near water. Be prepared to move to higher ground quickly. Never drive across flooded roads or trails. Turn around, don’t risk it. Watch for weather updates. Conditions can change rapidly.
If Caught in a Flash Flood:
Move immediately to higher ground.
Never walk or drive through moving water.
Call 911 in an emergency and provide your location.
Check the National Weather Service, local forecasts, or contact a ranger station for current information.
Bottom line: Conditions are dangerous near streams, rivers, and valleys. Be alert and ready to move uphill at the first sign of rising water.
For more information: https://www.facebook.com/share/1LV7FfvT7X/?mibextid=wwXIfr
